episodes.213897: Increasing monsoon moisture across western and north central New Mexico combined with daytime heating resulted in the development of showers and thunderstorms across the western and northern mountains midday July 14th before slowly drifting south and southwest over nearby lower elevations. Outflow from thunderstorms moving south off the San Juan Mountains in southwest Colorado resulted in a brief 58 mph wind gust at a mesonet station in Aztec. Showers and thunderstorms across western and north central NM tapered off during the early to mid evening hours due to the loss of daytime heating.
episodes.214124: Scattered thunderstorm activity developed during the afternoon hours across the higher terrain areas of eastern AZ from the Mogollon Rim southward through southeast AZ and were steered westward under easterly mid-level flow. These thunderstorms were fueled by MLCAPE of 1000-1500 J/KG. With DCAPE values near 1500 J/KG, the environment was conducive to strong downburst winds as well as strong outflows. A complex of thunderstorms materialized across eastern Pinal County by the late afternoon, with a strong outflow emanating from the complex moving westward into the Phoenix metro area. The outflow generated areas of blowing dust (locally dense in some areas) as well as additional thunderstorm activity across portions of the Phoenix area. Peak wind gusts between 35-55 mph were observed as the outflow surged westward through Phoenix. Tree damage in the form of broken branches as well as downed power poles and powerlines were reported across some areas.
episodes.214289: The frontal boundary from 7/12 remained stalled near the southeastern Midlands of SC into the CSRA through the day on 7/13. The environment in proximity to this front was conducive for flash flooding as slow moving convection exhibited efficient rain rates up to 2-4/hr. This brought flash flooding across Evans and Martinez GA during the evening  with additional locations of flash flooding in the Midlands of SC.
episodes.214583: Storms produced heavy rainfall and flash flooding across portions of Southeast Texas.
episodes.214712: The slow-moving trough continued to make its way towards the region on July 14th. Once again, heavy rainfall led to continued flash flooding across Terrell County.
episodes.214774: The synoptic pattern shifted by mid July sufficiently to allow a more marked influx of monsoonal moisture into Utah. In addition to some isolated thunderstorm wind gusts, this resulted in numerous instances of flash flooding and debris flows.
episodes.214951: Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced several wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.215251: An upper level shortwave and surface cold front moved across a moderately unstable airmass across Ontario province and northern NY during the late evening/overnight hours of July 14th-15th and then moved across VT.||Numerous thunderstorms entered central and southern VT from NY state with several of them producing significant severe weather in terms of damaging winds in Addison, Rutland and Windsor counties.||Earlier in the day, a renegade thunderstorm from Quebec moved across northeast VT and produced localized minor wind damage.
episodes.215485: A surge of deeper monsoonal moisture spread across western NV and eastern CA on the 13th and 14th produced widespread wetting rainfall totals of 0.10��� to nearly 1���. On July 13th, storms produced about 45 minutes of very heavy rainfall in NW Reno that led to some minor street flooding along Keystone and Washington avenues.
episodes.215585: A large cluster of thunderstorms produced very heavy rainfall in the Savannah metro area in the late afternoon hours. Rain gages around the area reported 2 to 3 inches of rain in a 2 to 3 hour period of time, including a USGS rain gage near Richmond Hill which reported 2.26 inches of rain in an hour including 1.97 inches of rain that fell in just 30 minutes. The intense rainfall led to several instances of flash flooding around Savannah.
episodes.215718: A strong upper-level ridge moved over the northern Great Plains allowing a moist, tropical airmass to move over South-Central Texas. Precipitable water values increased to greater than 2.0 inches which were near or above the 95th percentile of climatological values for this part of July. Multiple rounds of excessive rainfall were triggered by mid-level disturbances around the southern periphery of the high and low-level outflow boundaries. This convection was aided by nocturnal low-level jet streaks which led to slow moving, back building thunderstorms. Most of South-Central Texas received more than two inches of rain. The greatest totals were over Uvalde and Kinney Counties where 20-30 inches occurred. Another local maximum of 15-20 inches was observed in central Kerr County. Ten to 15 inches were widespread from Del Rio to Hondo and northward to northeastern Edwards to western Gillespie Counties. Damage estimates were near $115 million across South-Central Texas.
episodes.216519: An upper-level disturbance and increasing monsoonal moisture brought scattered showers and thunderstorms to the region. The convective environment was favorable to produce severe thunderstorms with large hail greater than 2 and isolated flash flooding.
episodes.216522: Southwest flow mainly focus isolated strong to severe convection over the I-95 corridor and Atlantic coast. Presence of dry air aloft likely played into stronger downbursts and areas of wind damage across northeast FL.
episodes.216588: Onshore westerly sea breeze flow and a shortwave aloft swinging across the SE U.S. combined to produce a broken line of convection that produced strong marine wind gusts near the mouth of Tampa Bay and over the Nature Coast waters near Cedar Key.
episodes.216665: During mid-July, a slow-moving easterly wave brought sufficient moisture and lift to trigger showers and thunderstorms across portions of Central and North Texas. Flash flooding occurred in multiple areas due to the influx of tropical moisture, weak flow aloft, and slow storm movement.
episodes.216844: Thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts along the east central Florida coast.
episodes.216868: A stationary front was convectively reinforced south across East Texas to just north of the I-20 corridor, as well as North Louisiana during the morning hours of July 13th, ahead of bands of showers and thunderstorms that developed and moved east along the front from North into East Texas. The morning storms produced heavy rainfall which led to localized flooding in Smith County before diminishing, although the presence of the surface boundary and a weak upper level disturbance extending from Eastern Texas across North Louisiana into the Tennessee Valley contributed to large scale forcing within a hot, moist, and unstable air mass for the development of additional showers and thunderstorms across these areas during the mid and late afternoon. Given the weak steering currents, these storms were slow moving, and produced very heavy rainfall in a short period of time, leading to instances of flash flooding across portions of East Texas and Northwest Louisiana. Rainfall totals of 1-3 inches, with isolated totals in excess of 6 inches, were observed before the storms diminished during the evening.
episodes.216893: A slow moving storm system and abundant tropical moisture resulted in flash flooding across mainly the Northwest Hill Country and Northern Edwards Plateau.
episodes.216897: Upper level troughing remained over southwest Louisiana during multiple days in mid July. This allowed scattered storms to develop each day with some producing heavy rain.
episodes.216932: A slow-moving frontal boundary was stalled north of the Gulf Coast. At the same time,  an upper-level weakness maintained an unusually active marine convective pattern. With relatively weak background winds, the primary hazards over the coastal waters came from thunderstorms. Repeated clusters of convection produced localized strong wind gusts across the offshore waters.
episodes.217293: Continuing an active monsoon period with multiple recorded wind gusts of 50 to 62 mph in Pima, Cochise, and Pinal counties. The severe thunderstorm winds caused damage to power equipment that caused power outages in Bisbee. Additionally, the heavy rainfall caused running washes that led to 1 water rescue in the Tucson Metro and impassable roadways.
episodes.217294: Continuing an active monsoon period with multiple recorded wind gusts of 48 to 52 mph in Pima, Cochise, and Pinal counties. The severe thunderstorm winds caused damage to power equipment that caused power outages in Dudleyville. Additionally, the heavy rainfall caused running washes that led to 1 water rescue in the Tucson Metro and impassable roadways.
episodes.217327: Severe weather across New Hampshire on July 14-15th, 2026, was driven by an unusually potent, high-end severe setup, that was tampered by cloud cover and thick wildfire smoke from Canada.  An intense mid-level shortwave trough and an accompanying surface cold front pushed east-southeastward from Quebec and northern New York into New England. Strong wind shear (40���50+ kt deep-layer shear) paired with high storm-relative helicity supported organized supercells and embedded bowing segments.  The cloud cover and thick smoke inhibited development early in the day, but organized convection developed during the evening across Central and Northern New Hampshire and continued through the night into the early morning hours of July 15th.
episodes.217396: Damaging winds associated with isolated strong to marginally severe, mostly afternoon and evening, thunderstorms were observed across portions of central Mississippi. Heavy rains from slow moving thunderstorms resulted in isolated flash flooding.

events.narrative: Public reports and radar estimates indicated around 8 to 12 inches of rain fell in the D'Hanis area on the morning of July 14. Widespread flooding occurred in D'Hanis due to a combination of riverine flooding along Seco and Parker creeks and poor drainage following torrential rains. All roads in D'Hanis south of US90 had standing water and water was observed surrounding homes and businesses. However, no structures sustained floodwater inundation. The CR429 crossing over Seco Creek was flooded.

Heavy rain flooded streets in Sabinal beginning early on July 14, including Center St. At least two water rescues were reported in the area on July 14. A second round of heavy rain early on July 15 resulted in additional water rescues. US87 was flooded in spots between Sabinal and Utopia. TX127, RR187, and CR301 also experienced flooding. On July 16, the Sabinal River overtopped the TX127 bridge northwest of Sabinal. Around 2 ft of inundation was observed atop the RM1050 bridge over the Sabinal River in Utopia.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding on the Bexar/Comal County line. FM 1863 at Cibolo Creek was flooded and impassable.

Several roadways were flooded in the Concan and Reagan Wells area from July 14 through July 16. Roads around Garner State Park were closed. RR1051 in Reagan Wells saw at least 2ft of inundation. Crossings across the Frio River between 7 Bluffs Crossing and Kenneth Arthur Crossing were flooded. The Frio River overtopped the FM1050 bridge at Garner State Park and over TX127. Rises on the Dry Frio River overtopped six river crossings in Reagan Wells, causing some washouts. Several residences were flooded and residents were stranded for up to a week due to the flooded crossings.

Around 1 ft of water was observed over US90 around 2 miles east of Knippa early on July 14 resulting in impassable conditions and closure of the highway. Widespread inundation was observed in surrounding areas near Dinner Creek. The flooding ultimately washed out portions of US90 at Dinner Creek near CR304. Portions of the railroad along US90 necessitated repairs after some track ballast was washed out. Several other roads in the Knippa area took on water, including FM1049 in several locations and other county roads and farm-to-market roads. Additional heavy rain on July 15 and July 16 prolonged the flooding and impassable road conditions.

The Uvalde area and Leona River watershed received some of the heaviest rainfall in South-Central Texas during the July 2026 flood event. Rounds of torrential rain occurred each morning between July 14 and July 16. The headwaters of the Leona River saw 20 to 30 inches of rain during a 3-day stretch. CoCoRaHS observers reported 10 to 15 inches in the Uvalde area. ||Uvalde was among the areas most impacted by the flooding. Some homes experienced 3ft of inundation. An estimated 300 to 500 residents were displaced by flooding in Uvalde. Numerous water rescues occurred throughout the flood event. On the morning of July 16, a vehicle was swept off US83 near CR400 north of Uvalde along the Leona River, resulting in one fatality. The driver had reportedly eluded law enforcement warnings not to proceed up the roadway. Mandatory evacuations were ordered for residents along the Leona River during the event with broader voluntary evacuation orders, leading to the evacuation of hundreds of people. At one point, there were at least 256 people in shelters.||Damage to roads was widespread. TX55 sustained significant damage at several points due to rises on the Nueces River, particularly between Indian Creek Rd and CR410. Washouts were also reported on FM2369 and CR415. ||The Deer Valley area was hard hit on July 14, with multiple water rescues and evacuations reported as the area was cut off by flooding along CR428. Inundation of some homes was reported along Taylor Slough. Numerous roads were flooded and impassable in Uvalde proper, including portions of US90 and US83. Extensive flooding occurred around Uvalde Plaza near Taylor Slough, impacting businesses along Main St and Garner Field Rd. Extensive street flooding occurred again on July 15, surrounding homes in the Rio Seco subdivision. The flooding continued into July 16 with all major highways and streets near rivers, creeks, and sloughs in Uvalde closed due to flooding. Widespread inundation was observed with floodwaters reaching homes in the Rio Seco subdivision and along the Leona River near Studer St. Main St and other midtown neighborhoods were flooded by the Leona River. All three entrances from US83 into Uvalde Estates were impassable with flooding on all creeks and low water crossings in the area.

A member of the public reported heavy rainfall in the area. As rain continued to fall, conditions progressively got worse with an mPING report indicating localized flash flooding. An emergency management coordinator later reported that the city of Navasota had multiple roads closed, severe road and culvert damage from heavy rainfall. The following roads were closed across the county: HWY 6 near J5 Tractor southbound, FM 1227 near HWY 6 at the railroad, FM 1774 near St. Marys, FM 3090 near FM 3455, FM 3455 between Fairgrounds and HWY 90, CR 227, CR 229, CR 318, CR 405, CR 406, CR 409, FM 2 near Luther Unit, FM 362 at Beason Creek (approximately 3 ft over roadway), CR 302. Overall the worst flooding was largely confined to Navasota with isolated inundation across various other county roads over the region.
